Moscow is first mentioned in chronicles under the year 1147, as part of the principality of [Rostov-Suzdal](/wiki/Rostov-Suzdal "Rostov-Suzdal"), which emerged from the disintegration of [Kievan Rus'](/wiki/Kievan_Rus%27 "Kievan Rus'").[[39]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFennell202345-41) It was referred to as a meeting place of [Yuri Dolgorukiy](/wiki/Yuri_Dolgorukiy "Yuri Dolgorukiy") and [Sviatoslav Olgovich](/wiki/Sviatoslav_Olgovich "Sviatoslav Olgovich"). At the time, it was a minor town on the western border of the principality.[[40]](#cite_note-42) The importance of Moscow greatly increased during the second half of the 12th century, and it was converted into a fortified *gorod* (stronghold) in the 1150s, with the first walls of the [Kremlin](/wiki/Kremlin "Kremlin") being built.[[41]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFennell202346-43) During the [Mongol invasions](/wiki/Mongol_invasion_of_Kievan_Rus%27 "Mongol invasion of Kievan Rus'") of 1237–1238, Moscow was sacked following the destruction of [Ryazan](/wiki/Ryazan "Ryazan").[[41]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFennell202346-43)

The first prince of Moscow was [Daniel](/wiki/Daniel_of_Moscow "Daniel of Moscow"), the youngest son of [Alexander Nevsky](/wiki/Alexander_Nevsky "Alexander Nevsky"), and in 1263, he was given Moscow as an *[otchina](/wiki/Votchina "Votchina")* (hereditary land), where he established a local branch of [Rurikid](/wiki/Rurikids "Rurikids") princes.[[42]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFennell202347-44) Two chronicles refer to [Mikhail Khorobrit](/wiki/Mikhail_Khorobrit "Mikhail Khorobrit") as "Mikhail of Moscow" in the mid-13th century, but Daniel is generally considered to be the first prince of Moscow.[[42]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFennell202347-44) On Mikhail's death in 1248, if it is assumed that an [appanage](/wiki/Appanage "Appanage") principality was created, Moscow reverted as an esche

First international reviews were "unanimously positive".[[129]](#cite_note-136) [Caryn James](/wiki/Caryn_James "Caryn James") of the BBC, who rated it 5 out of 5 stars, felt the "most expansive and magisterial" Miyazaki film "amounts to a summing up of many strands of his long career" and its pace "never slows, and there is too much coming at Mahito for anyone to absorb in a single viewing".[[130]](#cite_note-137) Tomris Laffly, writing for *[TheWrap](/wiki/TheWrap "TheWrap")*, epitomized the film as a "swan song so personal, artful and ultimately timeless" and thought it was "the deepest and darkest Studio Ghibli film" since *[Grave of the Fireflies](/wiki/Grave_of_the_Fireflies "Grave of the Fireflies")*.[[131]](#cite_note-138) [David Ehrlich](/wiki/David_Ehrlich "David Ehrlich") of *IndieWire*, who gave the film an "A" rating, wrote that the film "finds Miyazaki so nakedly bidding adieu—to us, and to the crumbling kingdom of dreams and madness that he'll soon leave behind—that it somehow resolves into an even more fitting goodbye [than *The Wind Rises*], one graced with the divine awe and heart-stopping wistfulness of watching a true immortal make peace with their own death".[[132]](#cite_note-139) [IGN](/wiki/IGN "IGN")'s Rafael Motamayor reviewed *The Boy and the Heron* as Ghibli's "most visually complex film" and awarded it a score of 9 out of 10, where he expressed how Miyazaki has delivered an exceptional conclusion to his distinguished career through an animated adventure that reminds audiences of their fortune to witness Studio Ghibli's cinematic creations.[[133]](#cite_note-140) On a less positive side, *[The Guardian](/wiki/The_Guardian "The Guardian")* writer Radheyan Simonpillai, assigning the film 3 out of 5 stars, saw it as "a gentler and slower though no less soulful addition to his canon".[[134]](#cite_note-141)

fanoutqa_014013.x:
Tokyo :: Geography :: Climate :: part 01 :: chunk_0018
The former city of Tokyo and the majority of Tokyo prefecture lie in the [humid subtropical climate](/wiki/Humid_subtropical_climate "Humid subtropical climate") zone ([Köppen climate classification](/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification"): *Cfa*),[[103]](#cite_note-105) with hot, humid summers and cool winters with occasional cold spells. The region, like much of Japan, experiences a one-month [seasonal lag](/wiki/Seasonal_lag "Seasonal lag"). The warmest month is August, which averages 26.9 °C (80.4 °F). The coolest month is January, averaging 5.4 °C (41.7 °F). The record low temperature was −9.2 °C (15.4 °F) on January 13, 1876. The record high was 39.5 °C (103.1 °F) on July 20, 2004.
The record highest low temperature is 30.4 °C (86.7 °F), on August 11, 2013.[[104]](#cite_note-106)

Annual rainfall averages nearly 1,600 millimeters (63.0 in), with a wetter summer and a drier winter. The growing season in Tokyo lasts for about 322 days from around mid-February to early January.[[105]](#cite_note-107) Snowfall is sporadic and occurs almost annually.[[106]](#cite_note-108) Tokyo often sees typhoons every year, though few are strong. The wettest month since records began in 1876 was October 2004, with 780 millimeters (30 in) of rain,[[107]](#cite_note-109) including 270.5 mm (10.65 in) on the ninth of that month.[[108]](#cite_note-110) The most recent of four months on record to observe no precipitation is December 1995.[[109]](#cite_note-JMArecords-111) Annual precipitation has ranged from 879.5 mm (34.63 in) in 1984 to 2,229.6 mm (87.78 in) in 1938.[[109]](#cite_note-JMArecords-111)

Clinton befriended fellow American Rhodes Scholar Frank Aller during his time at Oxford. In 1969, Aller received a [draft](/wiki/Draft_lottery_(1969) "Draft lottery (1969)") letter that mandated deployment to the [Vietnam War](/wiki/Vietnam_War "Vietnam War"). China is the second most populous country in the world and its national population density (1000/km2) is very similar to [those](/wiki/List_of_countries_by_population_density "List of countries by population density") of countries like [Denmark](/wiki/Denmark "Denmark") (excluding Greenland) or the [Czech Republic](/wiki/Czech_Republic "Czech Republic"). However, the overall population density of China contains major regional variations. In 2002, about 94% of the population lived east of the [Heihe–Tengchong Line](/wiki/Heihe%E2%80%93Tengchong_Line "Heihe–Tengchong Line"); although this eastern area comprises only 43% of China's total land area, its population density, at roughly 280/km2, is comparable to that of Japan.[[24]](#cite_note-24)

Broadly speaking, the population concentrates east of the [Tibetan Plateau](/wiki/Tibetan_Plateau "Tibetan Plateau") and south of the [northern steppe](/wiki/Mongolian%E2%80%93Manchurian_grassland "Mongolian–Manchurian grassland"). Hawaii consists of 137 [volcanic islands](/wiki/Volcanic_island "Volcanic island") that make up almost the entire [Hawaiian archipelago](/wiki/Hawaiian_archipelago "Hawaiian archipelago") (the exception is [Midway Atoll](/wiki/Midway_Atoll "Midway Atoll")). Spanning 1,500 miles (2,400 km), the state is [physiographically](/wiki/Physical_geography "Physical geography") and [ethnologically](/wiki/Ethnology "Ethnology") part of the [Polynesian](/wiki/Polynesia "Polynesia") subregion of [Oceania](/wiki/Oceania "Oceania").[[12]](#cite_note-16) Hawaii's ocean coastline is consequently the [fourth-longest in the U.S.](/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_coastline "List of U.S. states and territories by coastline"), at about 750 miles (1,210 km).[[e]](#cite_note-17) The eight main islands, from northwest to southeast, are [Niʻihau](/wiki/Ni%CA%BBihau "Niʻihau"), [Kauaʻi](/wiki/Kaua%CA%BBi "Kauaʻi"), [Oʻahu](/wiki/O%CA%BBahu "Oʻahu"), [Molokaʻi](/wiki/Moloka%CA%BBi "Molokaʻi"), [Lānaʻi](/wiki/L%C4%81na%CA%BBi "Lānaʻi"), [Kahoʻolawe](/wiki/Kaho%CA%BBolawe "Kahoʻolawe"), [Maui](/wiki/Maui "Maui"), and [Hawaiʻi](/wiki/Hawai%CA%BBi_(island) "Hawaiʻi (island)"), after which the state is named; the last is often called the "Big Island" or "Hawaiʻi Island" to avoid confusion with the state or archipelago. The uninhabited [Northwestern Hawaiian Islands](/wiki/Northwestern_Hawaiian_Islands "Northwestern Hawaiian Islands") make up most of the [Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument](/wiki/Papah%C4%81naumoku%C4%81kea_Marine_National_Monument "Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument"), the [largest protected area](/wiki/List_of_national_monuments_of_the_United_States "List of national monuments of the United States") in the U.S. and the [fourth-largest](/wiki/List_of_largest_protected_areas "List of largest protected areas") in the world.

At the highest estimates, this would make *Perucetus* the heaviest known animal in history,[[11]](#cite_note-BianucciEtAl-11) although more recent estimates put it at a more moderate 60 to 113 tonnes[[12]](#cite_note-Lve_Science-12)or 35 to 40 tonnes[[13]](#cite_note-:2-13)

Breyer became a [federal judge](/wiki/United_States_federal_judge "United States federal judge") in 1980, when he was appointed to the [U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit](/wiki/United_States_Court_of_Appeals_for_the_First_Circuit "United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit"). In his 2005 book *[Active Liberty](/wiki/Active_Liberty "Active Liberty")*, Breyer made his first attempt to systematically communicate his views on legal theory, arguing that the judiciary should seek to resolve issues in a manner that encourages popular participation in governmental decisions.
